content_list.content_text: In 1976, the Cultural Revolution came to an end with the death of Chairman Mao. Few could have predicted that by the end of the 1980s Chinese cinema would be producing some of the most original and acclaimed films in the world. The reopening of the Beijing Film Academy paved the way, and when the first class graduated in 1982, the so-called Fifth Generation of filmmakers was ready to lead a revolution in Chinese cinema.

information.contentText: Zhang Yimou, Chen's classmate, shot the film. Richard James Havis, author of Changing the Face of Chinese Cinema: An Interview with Chen Kaige, said the film was the first Chinese film "at least since the Communist Liberation of 1949, to tell a story through images rather than dialogue."

content_list.content_text: Meanwhile, the older directors of the Fourth Generation were already reassessing China's troubled past. Xie Jin (1923-2008) used melodrama to cast a look at the political persecutions of the Cultural Revolution in Tian Yun Shan Chuan Qi (Legend of Tianyun Mountain, 1980). They also adopted a more innovative way of filmmaking that resulted in a new realism.

quote.quote: By the end of A City of Sadness, you realize that Hou sees the world as it is, with all its contradictory brilliance.
quote.author: Glen Heath Jr. on A City of Sadness (1989)

content_list.content_text: Zhang Nuanxin (1941-1995), for example, opted for a semi-documentary style in Sha Ou (The Drive to Win, 1981). The Fourth Generation dealt with issues of contemporary relevance. In Xiangnu xiaoxiao (A Girl from Hunan, 1986), Xie Fei (b. 1942) showed the persistence of marriage traditions in rural regions.

information.contentTitle: Trailer for A City of Sadness
information.contentText: A City of Sadness was the first (of three) Taiwanese films to win the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, and it is often considered Hou's masterpiece. The film was selected as the Taiwanese entry for Best Foreign Language Film at the 62nd Academy Awards, but was not accepted as a nominee.

content_list.content_text: Moreover, as teachers at the Beijing Film Academy, the Fourth Generation directors would influence the next generation of filmmakers. In the words of Zhang Yingjin, "<i>Like their predecessors, the Fifth Generation favored a non-dramatic, depoliticized narrative structure, but went further with sparse dialogue and music, as well as an abundance of ambiguities in characterization and narrative. They insisted on showing their films rather than telling what happened."

Chen Kaige (b. 1952) made a visually stunning debut with Huang tu di (Yellow Earth, 1984) at the remote Guangxi studio, near the border with Vietnam. Zhang Yimou (b. 1951), who had worked as cinematographer on Chen's films, made his own debut with Hong Gao Liang (Red Sorghum, 1988), a harrowing account of Chinese history before the civil war.

information.contentText: Although it was produced on a tight budget and was relatively unknown until it hit screens (due to virtually no advertising), it broke Hong Kong's box office record and became a blockbuster in Asia.

content_list.content_text: Here, as in his later films, Zhang benefited from an intense performance by his star, Gong Li, and made great use of the complex visual symbolism of red - a color linked to fire and blood, but with traditional associations with happiness in China.

quote.quote: A Better Tomorrow is essential viewing for understanding the roots of John Woo's reputation as a master of action cinema.
quote.author: Ronald Perrone on A Better Tomorrow (1986)

content_list.content_text: Communism, however, did not dominate the entire Chinese-speaking world. Across the strait, the capitalist island of Taiwan was also experiencing a cinematic renaissance with the emergence of a creative and distinctive art cinema. The leading figures of this renaissance included Hou Hsiao-hsien (b. 1947), whose films are characterized by long sequences and long takes reminiscent of classic Japanese cinema. His most important work is, arguably, the Taiwan trilogy, which begins with Bei Qing Cheng Shi (A City of Sadness, 1989). The other notable director of the Taiwanese New Cinema was Edward Yang (1947-2007), whose film Kong bu fen zi (Terrorizers, 1986) strikingly explores the theme of urban angst.

information.contentText: Strong, lush colors saturate Red Sorghum, Zhang Yimou's exotic parable set in a sorghum wine distillery in the countryside.

content_list.content_text: Elsewhere in the Chinese-speaking world, John Woo (b. 1946) changed the face of Hong Kong cinema and profoundly influenced international cinema with the action thriller Ying Hung Boon Sik (A Better Tomorrow, 1986). This slick, stylized story of two rival brothers - a gangster and a cop - breathed new life into Chow Yun-fat's seemingly stalled career and broke box office records in Hong Kong.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacob, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: A Better Tomorrow
movies.overview: A reforming ex-gangster tries to reconcile with his estranged policeman brother, but the ties to his former gang are difficult to break.

movies.title: Yellow Earth
movies.overview: Yellow earth focuses on the story of a Communist soldier who is sent to the countryside to collect folk songs for the Communist Revolution. There he stays with a peasant family and learns that the happy songs he was sent to collect do not exist; the songs he finds are about hardship and suffering. He returns to the Army, but promises to come back for the young girl, Cuiqiao, who has been spellbound by his talk of the freedom women have under Communist rule and who wants to join the Communist Army.

movies.title: A City of Sadness
movies.overview: Soon after Japan relinquishes control of Taiwan in 1945, the Lin brothers face hardships from the changing culture. Bar owner Wen-heung, the eldest brother, falls foul of local gangsters, Wen-sun disappears, and Wen-leung, scarred by his experiences in the war, ends up in an insane asylum. Deaf-mute photographer Wen-ching, the youngest brother, decides to make a stand and fight the Kuomintang government from China that is assuming power.

movies.title: Terrorizers
movies.overview: The lives of a couple, an amateur photographer and an injured girl intertwine.

movies.title: Red Sorghum
movies.overview: An old leper who owned a remote sorghum winery dies. Jiu'er, the wife bought by the leper, and her lover, identified only as "my Grandpa" by the narrator, take over the winery and set up an idealized quasi-matriarchal community headed by Jiu'er. When the Japanese invaders subject the area to their rule and cut down the sorghum to make way for a road, the community rises up and resists as the sorghum grows anew.

movies.title: The Boys from Fengkuei
movies.overview: Ah-Ching and his friends have just finished school in their island fishing village, and now spend most of their time drinking and fighting. Three of them decide to go to the port city of Kaohsiung to look for work. They find an apartment through relatives, and Ah-Ching is attracted to the girlfriend of a neighbor. There they face the harsh realities of the big city.

movies.title: A Summer at Grandpa's
movies.overview: A coming-of-age story about a young brother and sister whom spend a pivotal summer in the country with their grandparents.

movies.title: Taipei Story
movies.overview: A young woman urgently seeks to navigate the maze of contemporary Taipei and find a future. She hopes that her boyfriend Lung is the key to the future, but Lung is stuck in a past that combines baseball and traditional loyalty that leads him to squander his nest egg bailing her father out of financial trouble.

movies.title: Hibiscus Town
movies.overview: Based on a novel by the same name written by Gu Hua, a melodrama about the life and travails of a young woman who lives through the turmoil of the Cultural Revolution.

movies.title: Ju Dou
movies.overview: A woman married to the brutal and infertile owner of a dye mill in rural China conceives a boy with her husband's nephew but is forced to raise her son as her husband's heir without revealing his parentage in this circular tragedy. Filmed in glowing technicolour, this tale of romantic and familial love in the face of unbreakable tradition is more universal than its setting.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1970 to 1989
content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies.
